title: Agents, codebases, and teams — Aditya Khandelwal, Amazon AGI Lab

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is harness engineering for team-wide agent adoption: progressive disclosure as a foundational practice, the ship-it skill as a high-value harness component handling code-done to PR-ready, smart prompt injection treating the codebase as a context feed, self-healing systems (nightly code gardener), and closing the loop with CI/CD and agentic reviews. The speaker explicitly names 'harness engineering principles' as a discipline and frames the entire problem as engineering the control plane around agents rather than the agents themselves.

secondary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
secondary.rationale: The application domain throughout is software engineering: the ship-it skill carries changes from code-done to PR-ready (descriptions, review comments, CI failures), the code gardener maintains codebase organization nightly, agentic reviews automate code review, and issues/boards are wired into the repo. The team ships 10+ PRs/day via these coding agents.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: Progressive disclosure is named as the foundational practice, with concrete context-management rules: keep skill.md under 100 lines, make the top-level agent MD a thin index, and measure first-prompt context burn (20-25K baseline, 40-50K indicates failure). Auto-compaction at 500k-1M tokens is a key symptom of a broken setup.

secondary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
secondary.rationale: Team adoption is framed along fear and confidence axes, with strategies for winning skeptics, managing day-to-day variation on the spectrum, and treating adoption as a human problem where fear is real. The leadership and cultural dimensions of agent adoption are significant secondary themes.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The talk is entirely about coding assistants in practice: PR agents, code gardeners, agentic reviews, and the ship-it skill for software engineering workflows.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The harness engineering practices—CLAUDE.md, skill.md, progressive disclosure, context burn measurement—are developer tooling that software builders use to work with agents.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: Team adoption, leadership intervention, shared setup governance, and the fear-confidence management framework are enterprise operational practices for scaling agent usage across a team.

summary: Aditya Khandelwal, Member of Technical Staff at Amazon AGI Labs, presents a playbook for team-wide adoption of AI coding agents based on his experience leading a 10-person team. He argues that solo-agent setup advice breaks in production team environments because the most impactful changes—restructuring codebases, converging on shared practices—require leadership and team buy-in, not individual initiative. He frames adoption along two axes: fear (job security concerns vs. seeing agents as tools) and confidence (effective utilization), with the goal of moving everyone to low-fear, high-utilization. Key symptoms of a broken setup include babysitting agents, burning 500K+ context on simple tasks hitting auto-compaction, complaining the model got dumb when the harness changed underneath, long sessions needing constant intervention, and slop factories. The review burden trap emerges when early adopters ship approximately 10 PRs/day while others ship 1-2 and absorb all review burden with worse code, reinforcing agent skepticism. His playbook centers on progressive disclosure as the foundational practice (skill.md under 100 lines, thin-index top-level MD, first-prompt context burn of 20-25K baseline with 40-50K indicating failure), a high-value ship-it skill handling code-done to PR-ready running over an hour, closing the loop with issues, agentic reviews, and a nightly code gardener, and winning skeptics by demonstrating trustworthy autonomy. He details failures—400-500 issues within weeks, agents filing incorrectly against each other, merge hell—and prescribes continuous iteration, prototype opt-outs from rigorous standards, and full commitment likened to skiing where pizza braking guarantees a crash. The mindset shift is from saying the model is dumb to asking how to make the shared setup smarter. The talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 at Moscone West, San Francisco.
whyItMatters: This talk is fundamentally about the gap between individual AI agent usage and team-scale production adoption. The software engineering concepts (progressive disclosure, ship-it skill, code gardener, CI/CD integration, shared setup) represent the concrete engineering practices that make agents productive in a real codebase. The AI concepts (harness engineering, smart prompt injection, self-healing systems, context burn diagnostics, fear-confidence framework) provide the theoretical and diagnostic lens for understanding why those practices work and how to evaluate them. Together they form a complete adoption loop: harness engineering principles define the discipline, progressive disclosure and context burn measurement provide the measurable design patterns, the ship-it skill and code gardener implement closing the loop, and the fear-confidence framework addresses the human side that determines whether any of it sticks. Without the engineering practices, the AI concepts remain abstract; without the AI diagnostic concepts, the engineering practices cannot be evaluated or iterated. The talk's central insight is that this integration is inherently a leadership problem because the practices require codebase restructuring and team convergence that no individual IC can achieve alone.
temporalContext: The talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026, held June 29 - July 2, 2026 at Moscone West, San Francisco. The video was published to the AI Engineer YouTube channel on August 11, 2026. Research was conducted on August 23-24, 2026. The talk reflects practices and experiences from leading a 10-person team through AI coding agent adoption, likely during the period between Amazon AGI SF Lab's formation in December 2024 and the conference in mid-2026. This places the content in the early-to-mid 2026 era of team-scale coding agent adoption, when tools like Claude Code and similar IDE-integrated agents were becoming production-grade but team-wide practices were still emerging.
takeaways: Solo agent setup advice breaks on real teams; team-wide adoption requires leadership, not individual initiative
Adoption should be framed along two axes: fear (job security) and confidence (effective utilization); the goal is moving everyone to low-fear, high-utilization
Symptoms of a bad setup include babysitting agents, 500k+ context burn on simple tasks, and blaming a dumb model when the harness changed
The review burden trap: early adopters ship ~10 PRs/day while others ship 1-2 and get stuck reviewing worse code, reinforcing agent skepticism
Progressive disclosure is the foundational practice—find best ICs' practices and propagate them as a shared setup across the team
One high-value ship it skill (code-done to PR-ready, running over an hour) convinced skeptics by demonstrating trustworthy autonomy
Agents taking too long is positive: it means you can do other things with confidence, and longer reasoning yields better output
Prototypes should opt out of rigorous standards; people vary on the fear-confidence spectrum day to day and need ongoing conversation
Commit fully to adoption—like skiing, partial commitment (pizza braking) guarantees a crash; be okay with failing and focus on recovery
Concrete progressive disclosure rules: keep skill.md under 100 lines, make the top-level agent MD a thin index, and measure first-prompt context burn (40-50K means it's failing)

concepts.name: Harness Engineering
concepts.explanation: The discipline of engineering the control plane around AI agents—including context management, prompt injection, self-healing systems, and continuous iteration—rather than focusing on the agents themselves. The talk explicitly names 'harness engineering principles' as a field of practice.
concepts.importance: The talk's primary subject and taxonomy classification. It reframes agent adoption from a model-quality problem to a harness-design problem, shifting focus to the engineering of tooling and context around agents.

concepts.name: Smart Prompt Injection
concepts.explanation: Treating the codebase itself as a mechanism for feeding context to agents at the right time, such as embedding runbooks in code comments so agents discover them naturally during code exploration.
concepts.importance: One of three named harness engineering principles. It provides a concrete technique for progressive disclosure by leveraging existing code structure rather than external configuration alone.

concepts.name: Self-Healing Agent Systems
concepts.explanation: Pipelines and routines that automatically detect and remove slop in agent-generated code, because slop is acknowledged as inevitable. The nightly code gardener is the concrete implementation.
concepts.importance: One of three named harness engineering principles. It addresses the reality that agent output quality cannot be perfect and requires automated remediation rather than manual oversight.

concepts.name: Auto-Compaction as Failure Signal
concepts.explanation: The behavior where agents silently burn through 500K to 1M tokens on simple tasks, hitting automatic context compaction. This is identified as a key symptom of a broken agent setup.
concepts.importance: Serves as a measurable diagnostic signal that progressive disclosure is failing, allowing teams to detect and fix context management problems before they cause broader adoption issues.

concepts.name: Fear-Confidence Adoption Framework
concepts.explanation: A two-axis model for understanding team member attitudes toward AI agents: fear (job security concerns vs. seeing agents as tools) and confidence (effective utilization). The goal is moving everyone to low-fear, high-utilization, recognizing that people vary on this spectrum day to day.
concepts.importance: Provides a structured framework for leaders to assess and manage the human side of agent adoption, going beyond technical configuration to address cultural and psychological barriers.

concepts.name: First-Prompt Context Burn Test
concepts.explanation: Measuring the token consumption of an agent's first prompt as a diagnostic for progressive disclosure effectiveness. 20-25K tokens is the baseline for a well-functioning setup; hitting 40-50K indicates progressive disclosure is failing.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete, quantifiable metric that teams can use to evaluate and iterate on their agent configurations, transforming an abstract practice into a measurable engineering discipline.

concepts.name: Longer Reasoning Yields Better Output
concepts.explanation: The counterintuitive finding that agents taking too long is actually positive—longer reasoning time correlates with better output quality. This reframes a perceived failure (agents being slow) as a feature, freeing humans to do other work with confidence.
concepts.importance: Challenges the common assumption that agent speed equals agent quality, providing a mental model shift that helps teams trust long-running autonomous agent tasks.

concepts.name: Babysitting Agents as Failure Mode
concepts.explanation: A pattern where engineers must constantly intervene in agent sessions, indicating the setup is not autonomous enough. Identified as a primary symptom of a broken agent setup.
concepts.importance: One of the key diagnostic signals teams should watch for, directly indicating that the harness engineering is insufficient and needs iteration.

concepts.name: Slop Factory
concepts.explanation: A state where an agent setup produces large volumes of low-quality code without proper review or quality controls, overwhelming the team's ability to maintain standards.
concepts.importance: Identifies a specific degradation mode that teams must prevent through self-healing pipelines and closing the loop practices.

concepts.name: Closing the Loop for Agent Systems
concepts.explanation: The practice of connecting agent output to issues, boards, agentic reviews, and nightly maintenance routines to create a continuous feedback system where agent work is validated, tracked, and improved over time.
concepts.importance: One of the four pillars of the adoption playbook, ensuring that agent output is not just generated but integrated into the team's quality and review processes.

concepts.name: Full Commitment to Agent Adoption
concepts.explanation: The principle that partial commitment to agent adoption guarantees failure, likened to skiing where 'pizza braking' (hesitation) causes crashes. Teams must commit fully, accept failure, and focus on recovery.
concepts.importance: Addresses the strategic and psychological dimension of adoption, warning against half-measures that produce the worst of both worlds—disruption without benefits.

concepts.name: Progressive Disclosure for Agent Configurations
concepts.explanation: Structuring agent context so information is revealed incrementally rather than loaded all at once. Concrete rules: keep skill.md files under 100 lines (a skill is really a folder), make the top-level agent MD file a thin index pointing to relevant files, and embed runbooks in code comments so agents discover them when exploring the codebase.
concepts.importance: Named as the foundational practice for team agent adoption. It is the primary diagnostic and corrective mechanism for context management problems, with measurable thresholds (20-25K baseline context burn, 40-50K failure threshold).

concepts.name: Ship It Skill (Code-Done to PR-Ready Pipeline)
concepts.explanation: A high-value autonomous agent skill that transforms code-done changes into PR-ready state by handling PR descriptions, review comments, and CI failure resolution. It runs for over an hour and convinced skeptics by demonstrating trustworthy agent autonomy.
concepts.importance: Serves as the keystone demonstration that agents can be trusted with long-running, high-stakes tasks. It was the concrete artifact that won over skeptical team members.

concepts.name: Nightly Code Gardener
concepts.explanation: An automated routine that runs nightly to check whether code is organized correctly, detect slop, and self-heal common structural issues in the codebase.
concepts.importance: Closes the loop on code quality by automating ongoing maintenance that would otherwise overwhelm human reviewers, addressing the inevitability of slop in agent-generated code.

concepts.name: CI/CD and Agentic Reviews Integration
concepts.explanation: Wiring CI/CD pipelines, agentic code reviews, and issue boards directly into the repository to create a closed feedback loop for agent-generated code.
concepts.importance: Part of the closing-the-loop practice that enables self-healing systems and ensures agent output is validated before merging.

concepts.name: Review Burden Trap
concepts.explanation: A failure pattern where early adopters ship approximately 10 PRs/day while others ship 1-2, leaving the slower members stuck reviewing worse code. This reinforces agent skepticism and creates a widening productivity gap within the team.
concepts.importance: Identifies a specific organizational dysfunction that arises without leadership intervention, explaining why individual adoption without team-wide practices leads to resentment and resistance.

concepts.name: Shared Setup vs Personal Setup
concepts.explanation: The principle that agent configuration must be a shared, team-invested resource rather than individual personal setups. Engineers should edit and iterate on the shared configuration collectively.
concepts.importance: Core to the talk's thesis that agent adoption is a leadership and team problem, not an individual IC problem. Without a shared setup, practices diverge and the review burden trap worsens.

concepts.name: CLAUDE.md as Thin Index Configuration
concepts.explanation: Using the top-level agent configuration file (CLAUDE.md) as a thin index that points to relevant files rather than an overloaded blob containing everything. This is a concrete implementation of progressive disclosure.
concepts.importance: Provides a specific, measurable design pattern for agent configuration files that prevents context overload and supports scalable team-wide adoption.

concepts.name: Issue Management at Agent Scale
concepts.explanation: Managing the explosion of issues when agents file them incorrectly against each other, causing the repo to blow up to 400-500 issues within a couple of weeks. Requires structural fixes to how agents interact with issue boards.
concepts.importance: A documented failure mode that teams must anticipate and manage, illustrating the operational challenges of scaling agent usage.

concepts.name: Prototype Opt-Out from Rigorous Standards
concepts.explanation: Allowing prototype and experimental code to opt out of the rigorous harness engineering standards that production code must follow, creating a two-tier system for code quality.
concepts.importance: Prevents the all-or-nothing mentality that blocks experimentation while maintaining quality for production code.

concepts.name: Merge Hell Management
concepts.explanation: The constant merge conflicts caused by high volumes of concurrently generated PRs from agents. The talk acknowledges this as unavoidable and something that must be managed rather than eliminated.
concepts.importance: A practical operational challenge that teams adopting agents at scale will face, requiring process and tooling solutions.

sections.title: Why solo agent advice breaks on a team
sections.summary: Khandelwal introduces the core problem: abundant content exists for individual agent setups, but it breaks when applied to team production environments. He led a 10-person team and found a working solution he wants to share.

sections.title: The enterprise adoption journey
sections.summary: Traces the journey from early excitement and outsized leverage, through mandates and token-maxing, to AI slop and sev-twos, to budget realities as token costs climbed and money had to be accounted for.

sections.title: Fear vs confidence: the two axes
sections.summary: Frames adoption along two axes: fear (job security concern vs. handy tool) and confidence/execution (how much people use agents effectively). The goal is moving everyone to low-fear, high-utilization. Describes how the team moved through stages from high-fear/low-utilization to skepticism as slop shipped.

sections.title: Is a CLAUDE.md and skills enough?
sections.summary: Poses the question of whether creating a CLAUDE.md and adding some skills solves the problem, asserting that life is messier than that and introducing the need to recognize symptoms of a broken setup.

sections.title: Symptoms your setup is wrong
sections.summary: Lists symptoms: babysitting agents, claiming the model got dumb when the harness changed, silently burning 500k+ context on simple tasks hitting auto-compaction, long sessions needing constant intervention, slop factories, and wondering how other companies ship so fast.

sections.title: Why this is leadership's job, not an IC's
sections.summary: Argues that making engineers work well with agents is the most impactful organizational priority. The review burden trap: early adopters ship 10 PRs/day, others ship 1-2 and get stuck reviewing bad code, reinforcing agent skepticism. Codebase restructuring requires team buy-in that only leadership can provide.

sections.title: Harness engineering principles
sections.summary: Covers three principles: smart prompt injection (treating the codebase as a way to feed context at the right time), closing the loop with self-healing systems because slop is inevitable, and continuous iteration. Emphasizes treating adoption as a human problem where fear is real.

sections.title: The playbook: basics, ship it, and closing the loop
sections.summary: Shares the playbook: do the basics with progressive disclosure by finding best ICs' practices and propagating them; invest in one high-value ship it skill handling code-done to PR-ready (descriptions, comments, CI failures), running over an hour; close the loop with issues, boards, CI/CD, agentic reviews, and a nightly code gardener; and win over skeptics by demonstrating value.

sections.title: Iterating on the shared setup
sections.summary: Emphasizes getting people to edit and play with the shared setup as proof of investment. Engineers must accept that the setup will never reach perfection and that X% of IC time should go to iterating on it, even without immediate meaningful PRs. Treats it as a continuous feedback loop.

sections.title: What went wrong along the way
sections.summary: Details problems faced: repo blew up to 400-500 issues within a couple weeks, agents filed issues incorrectly, people reverted to babysitting when things weren't perfect, agents took too long (reframed as positive—longer reasoning yields better output), and merge hell was constant.

sections.title: Prototypes, spectrums, and the shared setup mindset
sections.summary: Slop from experiments should be treated as prototypes that opt out of rigorous standards. People vary on the fear-confidence spectrum daily and need ongoing conversation. The mindset shift: instead of saying the model is dumb, ask how to make the shared setup smarter. It is not a personal setup but a shared one.

sections.title: Commit to the turn
sections.summary: Uses a skiing analogy to urge full commitment: pizza braking guarantees a crash, you must commit to the speed to turn and truly ski. Similarly, go full send with agent adoption, be okay with failing, and focus on recovery. That is how you truly feel the AGI.

sections.title: Q&A: Strategies for progressive disclosure
sections.summary: Recommends keeping skill.md files under 100 lines since a skill is really a folder. Embed runbooks in code comments so agents discover them. Make the top-level agent MD file a thin index pointing to the right files, not an overloaded blob. Test effectiveness by measuring first-prompt context burn: 20-25K is baseline, but hitting 40-50K means progressive disclosure is failing. Iterate based on these boundaries.

organization.name: Amazon AGI Labs
organization.summary: Amazon AGI Labs (also referred to as Amazon Artificial General Intelligence or AGI Lab) is Amazon's research organization dedicated to building useful AI agents that can take actions in digital and physical worlds. The lab is led by David Luan, VP of Autonomy, and was expanded with the formation of the AGI SF Lab in San Francisco in December 2024. The team develops Amazon Nova foundation models and the Amazon Nova Act agent platform, and conducts research in reinforcement learning for computer-use agents, tool calling, and agent reliability. Aditya Khandelwal is a Member of Technical Staff at AGI Labs.
